entries.0abc2082dc2c2047eeb4d4c6be71aa0a5d3bf0b3: <div sID="gen7477" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="2Kgs.19" sID="2Kgs.19"/> <div eID="gen7477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7478" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7479" type="x-p"/> Jerusalem's great distress we read of in the foregoing chapter, and left it besieged, insulted, threatened, terrified, and just ready to be swallowed up by the Assyrian army. But in this chapter we have an account of its glorious deliverance, not by sword or bow, but by prayer and prophecy, and by the hand of an angel. I. Hezekiah, in great concern, sent to the prophet Isaiah, to desire his prayers (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.1-2Kgs.19.5">ver. 1-5</reference>) and received from him an answer of peace, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.6-2Kgs.19.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. II. Sennacherib sent a letter to Hezekiah to fright him into a surrender, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.8-2Kgs.19.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. III. Hezekiah thereupon, by a very solemn prayer, recommended his case to God, the righteous Judge, and begged help from him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14-2Kgs.19.19">ver. 14-19</reference>. IV. God, by Isaiah, sent him a very comfortable message, assuring him of deliverance, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.20-2Kgs.19.34">ver. 20-34</reference>. V. The army of the Assyrians was all cut off by an angel and Sennacherib himself slain by his own sons, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35-2Kgs.19.37">ver. 35-37</reference>. And so God glorified himself and saved his people.
entries.f74da663686bbd7ae60c547e89404bfa7c627acb: <div eID="gen7479" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7478" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Hezekiah's Sends to Isaiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen7480" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass, when king Hezekiah heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> that he rent his clothes, and covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> And he sent Eliakim, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they said unto him, Thus saith Hezekiah, This day <hi type="italic">is</hi> a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and blasphemy: for the children are come to the birth, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> not strength to bring forth. <hi type="super">4</hi> It may be the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God will hear all the words of Rab-shakeh, whom the king of Assyria his master hath sent to reproach the living God; and will reprove the words which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath heard: wherefore lift up <hi type="italic">thy</hi> prayer for the remnant that are left. <hi type="super">5</hi> So the servants of king Hezekiah came to <reference osisRef="Isa.6">Isaiah.   6</reference> And Isaiah said unto them, Thus shall ye say to your master, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me. <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumour, and shall return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land. <div eID="gen7480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7481" type="x-p"/> The contents of Rabshakeh's speech being brought to Hezekiah, one would have expected (and it is likely Rabshakeh did expect) that he would call a council of war and it would be debated whether it was best to capitulate or no. Before the siege, he had <hi type="italic">taken counsel with his princes and his mighty men,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.3">2 Chron. xxxii. 3</reference>. But that would not do now; his greatest relief is that he has a God to go to, and what passed between him and his God on this occasion we have here an account of. <div eID="gen7481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7482" type="x-p"/> I. Hezekiah discovered a deep concern at the dishonour done to God by Rabshakeh's blasphemy. When he heard it, though at second hand, he <hi type="italic">rent his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.1">v. 1</reference>. Good men were wont to do so when they heard of any reproach cast on God's name; and great men must not think it any disparagement to them to sympathize with the injured honour of the great God. Royal robes are not too good to be rent, nor royal flesh too good to be clothed with sackcloth, in humiliation for indignities done to God and for the perils and terrors of his Jerusalem. To this God now called, and was displeased with those who were not thus affected. <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.14">Isa. xxii. 12-14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen and killing sheep,</hi> though it was a <hi type="italic">day of trouble and perplexity in the valley of vision</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.5">v. 5</reference>), which refers to this very event. The king was in sackcloth, but many of his subjects were in soft clothing. <div eID="gen7482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7483" type="x-p"/> II. He <hi type="italic">went up to the house of the Lord,</hi> according to the example of the psalmist, who, when he was grieved at the pride and prosperity of the wicked, <hi type="italic">went into the sanctuary of God</hi> and there <hi type="italic">understood their end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>. He went to the house of God, to meditate and pray, and get his spirit into a sedate composed frame, after this agitation. He was not considering what answer to return to Rabshakeh, but refers the matter to God. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt answer, Lord, for me.</hi>"—Herbert. In the house of the Lord he found a place both of rest and refuge, a treasury, a magazine, a council-chamber, and all he needed, all in God. Note, When the church's enemies are very daring and threatening it is the wisdom and duty of the church's friends to apply to God, appeal to him, and leave their cause with him. <div eID="gen7483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7484" type="x-p"/> III. He sent to the prophet Isaiah, by honourable messengers, in token of the great respect he had for him, to desire his prayers, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.2-2Kgs.19.4">v. 2-4</reference>. Eliakim and Shebna were two of those that had heard the words of Rabshakeh and were the better able both to acquaint and to affect Isaiah with the case. The elders of the priests were themselves to pray for the people in time of trouble (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.17">Joel ii. 17</reference>); but they must go to engage Isaiah's prayers, because he could pray better and had a better interest in heaven. The messengers were to go in sackcloth, because they were to represent the king, who was so clothed. <div eID="gen7484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7485" type="x-p"/> 1. Their errand to Isaiah was, "<hi type="italic">Lift up thy prayer for the remnant that is left,</hi> that is, for Judah, which is but a remnant now that the ten tribes are gone—for Jerusalem, which is but a remnant now that the defenced cities of Judah are taken." Note, (1.) It is very desirable, and what we should be desirous of when we are in trouble, to have the prayers of our friends for us. In begging to have them we honour God, we honour prayer, and we honour our brethren. (2.) When we desire the prayers of others for us we must not think we are excused from praying for ourselves. When Hezekiah sent to Isaiah to pray for him he himself <hi type="italic">went into the house of the Lord</hi> to offer up his own prayers. (3.) Those who speak from God to us we should in a particular manner desire to speak to God for us. <hi type="italic">He is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen. xx. 7</reference>. The great prophet is the great intercessor. (4.) Those are likely to prevail with God that <hi type="italic">lift up</hi> their prayers, that is, that lift up their hearts in prayer. (5.) When the interests of God's church are brought very low, so that there is but a remnant left, few friends, and those weak and at a loss, then it is time to <hi type="italic">lift up our prayer for that remnant.</hi> <div eID="gen7485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7486" type="x-p"/> 2. Two things are urged to Isaiah, to engage his prayers for them:—(1.) Their fears of the enemy (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.3">v. 3</reference>): "He is insolent and haughty; it is <hi type="italic">a day of rebuke and blasphemy.</hi> We are despised. God is dishonoured. Upon this account it is a day of trouble. Never were such a king and kingdom so trampled on and abused as we are: <hi type="italic">our soul is exceedingly filled with the contempt of the proud,</hi> and it is <hi type="italic">a sword in our bones</hi> to hear them reproach our confidence in God, and say, Where is now your God? and, which is worst of all, we see not which way we can help ourselves and get clear of the reproach. Our cause is good, our people are faithful; but we are quite overpowered with numbers. The children are brought to the birth; now is the time, the critical moment, when, if ever, we must be relieved. One successful blow given to the enemy would accomplish our wishes. But, alas! we are not able to give it: <hi type="italic">There is not strength to bring forth.</hi> Our case is as deplorable, and calls for as speedy help, as that of a woman in travail, that is quite spent with her throes, so that she has not strength to bear the child. Compare with this <reference osisRef="Hos.13.13">Hos. xiii. 13</reference>. We are ready to perish; <hi type="italic">if thou canst do any thing, have compassion upon us and help us.</hi>" (2.) Their hopes in God. To him they look, on him they depend, to appear for them. One word from him will turn the scale, and save the sinking remnant. If he but reprove the words of Rabshakeh (that is, disprove them, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.4">v. 4</reference>)—if he undertake to convince and confound the blasphemer—all will be well. And this they trust he will do, not for their merit's sake, but for his own honour's sake, because he has <hi type="italic">reproached the living God,</hi> by levelling him with deaf and dumb idols. They have reason to think the issue will be good, for they can interest God in the quarrel. <reference osisRef="Ps.74.22">Ps. lxxiv. 22</reference>, <hi type="italic">Arise O God! plead thy own cause.</hi> "He is the Lord thy God," say they to Isaiah—"<hi type="italic">thine,</hi> whose glory thou art concerned for, and whose favour thou art interested in. He has heard and known the blasphemous words of Rabshakeh, and therefore, it may be, he will hear and rebuke them. We hope he will. Help us with thy prayers to bring the cause before him, and then we are content to leave it with him." <div eID="gen7486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7487" type="x-p"/> IV. God, by Isaiah, sent to Hezekiah, to assure him that he would glorify himself in the ruin of the Assyrians. Hezekiah sent to Isaiah, not to enquire concerning the event, as many did that sent to the prophets (<hi type="italic">Shall I recover?</hi> or the like), but to desire his assistance in his duty. It was this that he was solicitous about; and therefore God let him know what the event should be, in recompence of his care to do his duty, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.6-2Kgs.19.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. 1. God interested himself in the cause: <hi type="italic">They have blasphemed me.</hi> 2. He encouraged Hezekiah, who was much dismayed: <hi type="italic">Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard;</hi> they are but words (though swelling and fiery words), and words are but wind. 3. He promised to frighten the king of Assyria worse than Rabshakeh had frightened him: "<hi type="italic">I will send a blast upon him</hi> (that pestilential breath which killed his army), upon which terrors shall seize him and drive him into his own country, where death shall meet him." This short threatening from the mouth of God would do execution, when all the impotent menaces that came from Rabshakeh's mouth would vanish into air.
entries.42f6a94dd22c0e0fee067b2bbd5010b194933437: <div eID="gen7487" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sennacherib Sends to Hezekiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen7488" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> So Rab-shakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah: for he had heard that he was departed from Lachish. <hi type="super">9</hi> And when he heard say of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, Behold, he is come out to fight against thee: he sent messengers again unto Hezekiah, saying, <hi type="super">10</hi> Thus shall ye speak to Hezekiah king of Judah, saying, Let not thy God in whom thou trustest deceive thee, saying, Jerusalem shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. <hi type="super">11</hi> Behold, thou hast heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, by destroying them utterly: and shalt thou be delivered? <hi type="super">12</hi> Have the gods of the nations delivered them which my fathers have destroyed; <hi type="italic">as</hi> Gozan, and Haran, and Rezeph, and the children of Eden which <hi type="italic">were</hi> in Thelasar? <hi type="super">13</hi> Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and Ivah? <hi type="super">14</hi> And Hezekiah received the letter of the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and spread it before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> And Hezekiah prayed before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of Israel, which dwellest <hi type="italic">between</hi> the cherubims, thou art the God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; thou hast made heaven and earth.   16 <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , bow down thine ear, and hear: open, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thine eyes, and see: and hear the words of Sennacherib, which hath sent him to reproach the living God. <hi type="super">17</hi> Of a truth, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the kings of Assyria have destroyed the nations and their lands, <hi type="super">18</hi> And have cast their gods into the fire: for they <hi type="italic">were</hi> no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now therefore, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> our God, I beseech thee, save thou us out of his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thou only. <div eID="gen7488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7489" type="x-p"/> Rabshakeh, having delivered his message and received no answer (whether he took this silence for a consent or a slight does not appear), left his army before Jerusalem, under the command of the other generals, and went himself to attend the king his master for further orders. He found him besieging Libnah, a city that had revolted from Judah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.22">ch. viii. 22</reference>. Whether he had taken Lachish or no is not certain; some think he departed from it because he found the taking of it impracticable, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.8">v. 8</reference>. However, he was now alarmed with the rumour that the king of the Cushites, who bordered upon the Arabians, was coming out against him with a great army, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.9">v. 9</reference>. This made him very desirous to gain Jerusalem with all speed. To take it by force would cost him more time and men than he could well spare, and therefore he renewed his attack upon Hezekiah to persuade him tamely to surrender it. Having found him an easy man once (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14">ch. xviii. 14</reference>), when he said, <hi type="italic">That which thou puttest on me I will bear,</hi> he hoped again to frighten him into a submission, but in vain. Here, <div eID="gen7489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7490" type="x-p"/> I. Sennacherib sent a letter to Hezekiah, a railing letter, a blaspheming letter, to persuade him to surrender Jerusalem, because it would be to no purpose for him to think of standing it out. His letter is to the same purport with Rabshakeh's speech; there is nothing new offered in it. Rabshakeh had said to the people, <hi type="italic">Let not Hezekiah deceive you,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.29">ch. xviii. 29</reference>. Sennacherib writes to Hezekiah, <hi type="italic">Let not thy God deceive thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.10">v. 10</reference>. Those that have the God of <hi type="italic">Jacob for their help, and whose hope is in the Lord their God,</hi> need not fear being deceived by him, as the heathen were by their gods. To terrify Hezekiah, and drive him from his anchor, he magnifies himself and his own achievements. See how proudly he boasts, 1. Of the lands he had conquered (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">All lands,</hi> and destroyed utterly! How are the mole-hills of his victories swelled to mountains! So far was he from destroying all lands that at this time the land of Cush, and Tirhakah its king, were a terror to him. What vast hyperboles may one expect in proud men's praises of themselves! 2. Of the gods he had conquered, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.12">v. 12</reference>. "Each vanquished nation and its gods, which were so far from being able to deliver them that they fell with them: and shall thy God deliver thee?" 3. Of the kings he had conquered (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.13">v. 13</reference>), the <hi type="italic">king of Hamath and the king of Arpad.</hi> Whether he means the prince or the idol, he means to make himself appear greater than either, and therefore very formidable, and the <hi type="italic">terror of the mighty in the land of the living.</hi> <div eID="gen7490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7491" type="x-p"/> II. Hezekiah encloses this in another letter, a praying letter, a believing letter, and sends it to the King of kings, who judges among the gods. Hezekiah was not so haughty as not to receive the letter, though we may suppose the superscription did not give him his due titles; when he had received it he was not so careless as not to read it; when he had read it he was not in such a passion as to write an answer to it in the same provoking language; but he immediately went up to the temple, presented himself, and then <hi type="italic">spread the letter before the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14">v. 14</reference>), not as if God needed to have the letter shown to him (he knew what was in it before Hezekiah did), but hereby he signified that he acknowledged God in all his ways,—that he desired not to aggravate the injuries his enemies did him nor to make them appear worse than they were, but desired they might be set in a true light,—and that he referred himself to God, and his righteous judgment, upon the whole matter. Hereby likewise he would affect himself in the prayer he came to the temple to make; and we have need of all possible helps to quicken us in that duty. In the prayer which Hezekiah prayed over this letter, 1. He adores the God whom Sennacherib had blasphemed (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.15">v. 15</reference>), calls him <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> because Israel was his peculiar people, and <hi type="italic">the God that dwelt between the cherubim,</hi> because there was the peculiar residence of his glory upon earth; but he gives glory to him as <hi type="italic">the God of the whole earth,</hi> and not, as Sennacherib fancied him to be, <hi type="italic">the God of Israel only,</hi> and confined to the temple. "Let them say what they will, thou art sovereign Lord, for thou art the God, the God of gods, sole Lord, even thou alone, universal Lord <hi type="italic">of all the kingdoms of the earth,</hi> and rightful Lord, <hi type="italic">for thou hast made heaven and earth.</hi> Being Creator of all, by an incontestable title thou art owner and ruler of all." 2. He appeals to God concerning the insolence and profaneness of Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, hear; Lord, see.</hi> Here it is under his own hand; here it is in black and white." Had Hezekiah only been abused, he would have passed it by; but it is God, the living God, that is reproached, the jealous God. <hi type="italic">Lord, what wilt thou do for thy great name?</hi> 3. He owns Sennacherib's triumphs over the gods of the heathen, but distinguishes between them and the God of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.17-2Kgs.19.18">v. 17, 18</reference>): He has indeed <hi type="italic">cast their gods into the fire;</hi> for <hi type="italic">they were no gods,</hi> unable to help either themselves or their worshipers, and therefore no wonder that he has destroyed them; and, in destroying them, though he knew it not, he really served the justice and jealousy of the God of Israel, who has determined to extirpate all the gods of the heathen. But those are deceived who think they can therefore be too hard for him. He is none of the gods whom men's hands have made, but he has himself made all things, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.3-Ps.115.4">Ps. cxv. 3, 4</reference>. 4. He prays that God will now glorify himself in the defeat of Sennacherib and the deliverance of Jerusalem out of his hands (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Now therefore save us;</hi> for if we be conquered, as other lands are, they will say that thou art conquered, as the gods of those lands were: but, Lord, distinguish thyself, by distinguishing us, and let all the world know, and be made to confess, that <hi type="italic">thou art the Lord God,</hi> the self-existent sovereign God, <hi type="italic">even thou only,</hi> and that all pretenders are vanity and a lie." Note, The best pleas in prayer are those which are taken from God's honour; and therefore the Lord's prayer begins with <hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name,</hi> and concludes with <hi type="italic">Thine is the glory.</hi>
entries.87bea76b3931fd1535300ad2f5c8aa2b7665e4ca: <div eID="gen7491" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sennacherib's Fall Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen7492" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, <hi type="italic">That</hi> which thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard. <hi type="super">21</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the word that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken concerning him; The virgin the daughter of Zion hath despised thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee. <hi type="super">22</hi> Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? and against whom hast thou exalted <hi type="italic">thy</hi> voice, and lifted up thine eyes on high? <hi type="italic">even</hi> against the Holy <hi type="italic">One</hi> of Israel. <hi type="super">23</hi> By thy messengers thou hast reproached the Lord, and hast said, With the multitude of my chariots I am come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon, and will cut down the tall cedar trees thereof, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the choice fir trees thereof: and I will enter into the lodgings of his borders, <hi type="italic">and into</hi> the forest of his Carmel. <hi type="super">24</hi> I have digged and drunk strange waters, and with the sole of my feet have I dried up all the rivers of besieged places. <hi type="super">25</hi> Hast thou not heard long ago <hi type="italic">how</hi> I have done it, <hi type="italic">and</hi> of ancient times that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities <hi type="italic">into</hi> ruinous heaps. <hi type="super">26</hi> Therefore their inhabitants were of small power, they were dismayed and confounded; they were <hi type="italic">as</hi> the grass of the field, and <hi type="italic">as</hi> the green herb, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the grass on the housetops, and <hi type="italic">as corn</hi> blasted before it be grown up. <hi type="super">27</hi> But I know thy abode, and thy going out, and thy coming in, and thy rage against me. <hi type="super">28</hi> Because thy rage against me and thy tumult is come up into mine ears, therefore I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest. <hi type="super">29</hi> And this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sign unto thee, Ye shall eat this year such things as grow of themselves, and in the second year that which springeth of the same; and in the third year sow ye, and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat the fruits thereof. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall yet again take root downward, and bear fruit upward. <hi type="super">31</hi> For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and they that escape out of mount Zion: the zeal of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">of hosts</hi> shall do this. <hi type="super">32</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> concerning the king of Assyria, He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shield, nor cast a bank against it. <hi type="super">33</hi> By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and shall not come into this city, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">34</hi> For I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake. <div eID="gen7492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7493" type="x-p"/> We have here the gracious copious answer which God gave to Hezekiah's prayer. The message which he sent him by the same hand (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.6-2Kgs.19.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), one would think, was an answer sufficient to his prayer; but, that he might have strong consolation, he was encouraged by two immutable things, <hi type="italic">in which it was impossible for God to lie,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 18</reference>. In general, God assured him that his prayer was heard, his prayer against Sennacherib, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.20">v. 20</reference>. Note, The case of those that have the prayers of God's people against them is miserable. For, if the oppressed cry to God against the oppressor, <hi type="italic">he will hear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.22.23">Exod. xxii. 23</reference>. God hears and answers, hears <hi type="italic">with the saving strength of his right hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Ps. xx. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen7493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7494" type="x-p"/> This message bespeaks two things:— <div eID="gen7494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7495" type="x-p"/> I. Confusion and shame to Sennacherib and his forces. It is here foretold that he should be humbled and broken. The prophet elegantly directs his speech to him, as he does, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Isa. x. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">O Assyrian! the rod of my anger.</hi> Not that this message was sent to him, but what is here said to him he was made to know by the event. Providence spoke it to him with a witness; and perhaps his own heart was made to whisper this to him: for God has more ways than one of speaking to sinners in his wrath, so as to <hi type="italic">vex them in his sore displeasure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.5">Ps. ii. 5</reference>. Sennacherib is here represented, <div eID="gen7495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7496" type="x-p"/> 1. As the scorn of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21">v. 21</reference>. He thought himself the terror of the daughter of Zion, that chaste and beautiful virgin, and that by his threats he could force her to submit to him: "But, being a virgin in her Father's house and under his protection, she defies thee, despises thee, laughs thee to scorn. Thy impotent malice is ridiculous; he that sits in heaven laughs at thee, and therefore so do those that abide under his shadow." By this word God intended to silence the fears of Hezekiah and his people. Though to an eye of sense the enemy looked formidable, to an eye of faith he looked despicable. <div eID="gen7496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7497" type="x-p"/> 2. As an enemy to God; and that was enough to make him miserable. Hezekiah pleaded this: "Lord, he has reproached thee," <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.16">v. 16</reference>. "He has," saith God, "and I take it as against myself (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whom hast thou reproached?</hi> Is it not the Holy One of Israel, whose honour is dear to him, and who has power to vindicate it, which the gods of the heathen have not?" <hi type="italic">Nemo me impune lacesset—No one shall provoke me with impunity.</hi> <div eID="gen7497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7498" type="x-p"/> 3. As a proud vainglorious fool, that spoke <hi type="italic">great swelling words of vanity,</hi> and <hi type="italic">boasted of a false gift,</hi> by his boasts, as well as by his threats, reproaching the Lord. For, (1.) He magnified his own achievements out of measure and quite above what really they were (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.23-2Kgs.19.24">v. 23, 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast said</hi> so and so. This was not in the letter he wrote, but God let Hezekiah know that he not only saw what was written there, but heard what he said elsewhere, probably in the speeches he made to his councils or armies. Note, God takes notice of the boasts of proud men, and will call them to an account, that he <hi type="italic">may look upon them and abuse them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.40.11">Job xl. 11</reference>. What a mighty figure does Sennacherib think he makes! Driving his chariots to the tops of the highest mountains, forcing his way through woods and rivers, breaking through all difficulties, making himself master of all he had a mind to. Nothing could stand before him or be withheld from him; no hills too high for him to climb, no trees too strong for him to fell, no waters too deep for him to dry up; as if he had the power of a God, to speak and it is done. (2.) He took to himself the glory of doing these great things, whereas they were all <hi type="italic">the Lord's doing,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.25-2Kgs.19.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. Sennacherib, in his letter, had appealed to what Hezekiah had heard (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast heard what the kings of Assyria have done;</hi> but, in answer to that, he is reminded of what God has done for Israel of old, drying up the Red Sea, leading them through the wilderness, planting them in Canaan. "What are all thy doings to these? And as for the desolations thou hast made in the earth, and particularly in Judah, thou art but the instrument in God's hand, a mere tool: it is <hi type="italic">I that have brought it to pass.</hi> I gave thee thy power, gave thee thy success, and made thee what thou art, raised thee up to lay waste fenced cities and so to punish them for their wickedness, and <hi type="italic">therefore their inhabitants were of small power.</hi>" What a foolish insolent thing was it for him to exalt himself above God, and against God, upon that which he had done by him and under him. Sennacherib's boasts here are expounded in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.13-Isa.10.14">Isa. x. 13, 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom,</hi> &c.; and they are answered (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.15">v. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith?</hi> It is surely absurd for the fly upon the wheel to say, What a dust do I make! or for the sword in the hand to say, What execution I do! If God be the principal agent in all that is done, boasting is for ever excluded. <div eID="gen7498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7499" type="x-p"/> 4. As under the check and rebuke of that God whom he blasphemed. All his motions were, (1.) Under the divine cognizance (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have thy abode,</hi> and what thou dost secretly devise and design, <hi type="italic">thy going out and coming in,</hi> marches and counter-marches, and <hi type="italic">thy rage against me</hi> and my people, the tumult of thy passions, the tumult of thy preparations, the noise and bluster thou makest: I know it all." That was more than Hezekiah did, who wished for intelligence of the enemy's motions; but what need was there for this when the eye of God was a constant spy upon him? <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>. (2.) Under the divine control (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will put my hook in thy nose,</hi> thou great Leviathan (<reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.41.2">Job xli. 1, 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">my bridle in thy jaws,</hi> thou great Behemoth. I will restrain thee, manage thee, turn thee where I please, send thee home like a fool as thou camest, <hi type="italic">re infecta</hi>—<hi type="italic">disappointed of thy aim.</hi>" Note, It is a great comfort to all the church's friends that God has a hook in the nose and a bridle in the jaws of all her enemies, can make even their wrath to serve and praise him and then restrain the remainder of it. <hi type="italic">Here shall its proud waves be stayed.</hi> <div eID="gen7499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7500" type="x-p"/> II. Salvation and joy to Hezekiah and his people. This shall be a sign to them of God's favour, and that he is reconciled to them, and <hi type="italic">his anger is turned away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Isa. xii. 1</reference>), a wonder in their eyes (for so a sign sometimes signifies), a token for good, and an earnest of the further mercy God has in store for them, that a good issue shall be put to their present distress in every respect. <div eID="gen7500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7501" type="x-p"/> 1. Provisions were scarce and dear; and what should they do for food? The fruits of the earth were devoured by the Assyrian army, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.9-Isa.32.10">Isa. xxxii. 9, 10</reference>, &c. Why, they shall not only dwell in the land, but <hi type="italic">verily they shall be fed.</hi> If God save them, he will not starve them, nor let them die by famine, when they have escaped the sword: "<hi type="italic">Eat you this year that which groweth of itself,</hi> and you shall find enough of that. Did the Assyrians reap what you sowed? You shall reap what you did not sow." But the next year was the sabbatical year, when the land was to rest, and they must neither sow nor reap. What must they do that year? Why, <hi type="italic">Jehovah-jireh—The Lord will provide.</hi> God's blessing shall save them seed and labour, and, that year too, the voluntary productions of the earth shall serve to maintain them, to remind them that the earth brought forth before there was a man to till it, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.11">Gen. i. 11</reference>. And then, the third year, their husbandry should return into its former channel, and they should sow and reap as they used to do. 2. The country was laid waste, families were broken up and scattered, and all was in confusion; how should it be otherwise when it was over-run by such an army? As to this, it is promised that <hi type="italic">the remnant that has escaped of the house of Judah</hi> (that is, of the country people) shall yet again be planted in their own habitations, upon their own estates, shall take root there, shall increase and grow rich, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.30">v. 30</reference>. See how their prosperity is described: it is <hi type="italic">taking root downwards,</hi> and <hi type="italic">bearing fruit upwards,</hi> being well fixed and well provided for themselves, and then doing good to others. Such is the prosperity of the soul: it is taking root downwards by faith in Christ, and then being fruitful in fruits of righteousness. 3. The city was shut up, none went out or came in; but now the remnant in Jerusalem and Zion shall go forth freely, and there shall be none to hinder them, or make them afraid, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.31">v. 31</reference>. Great destruction had been made both in city and country, bit in both there was a remnant that escaped, which typified the saved remnant of Israelites indeed (as appears by comparing <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22-Isa.10.23">Isa. x. 22, 23</reference>, which speaks of this very event, with <reference osisRef="Rom.9.27-Rom.9.28">Rom. ix. 27, 28</reference>), and they shall go forth into the glorious liberty of the children of God. 4. The Assyrians were advancing towards Jerusalem, and would in a little time besiege it in form, and it was in great danger of falling into their hands. But it is here promised that the siege they feared should be prevented,—that, though the enemy had now (as it should seem) encamped before the city, yet they should never <hi type="italic">come into the city,</hi> no, nor so much as <hi type="italic">shoot an arrow</hi> into it (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.32-2Kgs.19.33">v. 32, 33</reference>),—that he should be forced to retire with shame, and a thousand times to repent his undertaking. God himself undertakes to defend the city (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.34">v. 34</reference>), and that person, that place, cannot but be safe, the protection of which he undertakes. 5. The honour and truth of God are engaged for the doing of all this. These are great things, but how will they be effected? Why, <hi type="italic">the zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.31">v. 31</reference>. He is Lord of hosts, has all creatures at his beck, therefore he is able to do it; he is <hi type="italic">jealous for Jerusalem with great jealousy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.14">Zech. i. 14</reference>); having espoused her a chaste virgin to himself, he will not suffer her to be abused, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21">v. 21</reference>. "You have reason to think yourselves unworthy that such great things should be done for you; but God's own zeal will do it." His zeal, (1.) For his own honour (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.34">v. 34</reference>): "I will do it for my own sake, to make myself an everlasting name." God's reasons of mercy are fetched from within himself. (2.) For his own truth: "I will do it for my servant David's sake; not for the sake of his merit, but the promise made to him and the covenant made with him, those sure mercies of David." Thus all the deliverances of the church are wrought for the sake of Christ, the Son of David.
entries.56e22906eb06ff1abb04bf0dddc57180fb67256d: <div eID="gen7501" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Assyrian Army Destroyed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen7502" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they <hi type="italic">were</hi> all dead corpses. <hi type="super">36</hi> So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh. <hi type="super">37</hi> And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen7502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7503" type="x-p"/> Sometimes it was long ere prophecies were accomplished and promises performed; but here the word was no sooner spoken than the work was done. <div eID="gen7503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7504" type="x-p"/> I. The army of Assyria was entirely routed. That night which immediately followed the sending of this message to Hezekiah, when the enemy had just set down before the city and were preparing (as we now say) to open the trenches, that night was the main body of their army slain upon the spot by an angel, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">v. 35</reference>. Hezekiah had not force sufficient to sally out upon them and attack their camp, nor would God do it by sword or bow; but he sent his angel, a destroying angel, in the dead of the night, to make an assault upon them, which their sentinels, though ever so wakeful, could neither discover nor resist. It was <hi type="italic">not by the sword of a mighty man or of a mean man,</hi> that is, not of any man at all, but of an angel, that the Assyrians army was to fall (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.8">Isa. xxxi. 8</reference>), such an angel as slew the first-born of Egypt. Josephus says it was done by a pestilential disease, which was instant death to them. The number slain was very great, 185,000 men, and Rabshakeh, it is likely, among the rest. When the besieged <hi type="italic">arose, early in the morning, behold they were all dead corpses,</hi> scarcely a living man among them. Some think the <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12">76th Psalm</reference> was penned on this occasion, where we read that the <hi type="italic">stout-hearted were spoiled and slept their sleep,</hi> their last, their long sleep, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.5">v. 5</reference>. See how great, in power and might, the holy angels are, when one angel, in one night, could make so great a slaughter. See how weak the mightiest of men are before almighty God: who ever hardened himself against him and prospered? The pride and blasphemy of the king are punished by the destruction of his army. All these lives are sacrificed to God's glory and Zion's safety. The prophet shows that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> God suffered this vast rendezvous to be made, <hi type="italic">that they might be gathered as sheaves into the floor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.4.12-Mic.4.13">Mic. iv. 12, 13</reference>. <div eID="gen7504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7505" type="x-p"/> II. The king of Assyria was hereby put into the utmost confusion. Ashamed to see himself, after all his proud boasts, thus defeated and disabled to pursue his conquests and secure what he had (for this, we may suppose, was the flower of his army), and continually afraid of falling under the like stroke himself, <hi type="italic">He departed, and went, and returned;</hi> the manner of the expression intimates the great disorder and distraction of mind he was in, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.36">v. 36</reference>. And it was not long before God cut him off too, by the hands of <hi type="italic">two of his own sons,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.37">v. 37</reference>. 1. Those that did it were very wicked, to kill their own father (whom they were bound to protect) and in the act of his devotion; monstrous villany! But, 2. God was righteous in it. Justly are the sons suffered to rebel against their father that begat them, when he was in rebellion against the God that made him. Those whose children are undutiful to them ought to consider whether they have not been so to their Father in heaven. The God of Israel had done enough to convince him that he was the only true God, whom therefore he ought to worship; yet he persists in his idolatry, and seeks to his false god for protection against a God of irresistible power. Justly is his blood mingled with his sacrifices, since he will not be convinced by such a plain and dear-bought demonstration of his folly in worshipping idols. His sons that murdered him were suffered to escape, and no pursuit was made after them, his subjects perhaps being weary of the government of so proud a man and thinking themselves well rid of him. And his sons would be looked upon as the more excusable in what they had done if it be true (as bishop Patrick suggested) that he was now vowing to sacrifice them to his god, so that it was for their own preservation that they sacrificed him. His successor was another son, <hi type="italic">Esarhaddon,</hi> who (as it should seem) did not aim, like his father, to enlarge his conquests, but rather to improve them; for he it was that first sent colonies of Assyrians to inhabit the country of Samaria, though it is mentioned before (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.24">ch. xvii. 24</reference>), as appears, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">Ezra iv. 2</reference>, where the Samaritans say it was <hi type="italic">Esarhaddon that brought them thither.</hi>  <chapter eID="2Kgs.19"/> <div eID="gen7505" type="x-p"/>

entries.f55ebfcb500edcc875d295e12bf6ad7b62722fb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3539"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <div sID="gen5030" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.1-2Kgs.19.5">2Ki 19:1-5</reference>. Hezekiah in Deep Affliction.<div eID="gen5030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3539"/><hi type="bold">1-3. when king Hezekiah heard it, he rent his clothes--</hi>The rending of his clothes was a mode of expressing horror at the daring blasphemy--the assumption of sackcloth a sign of his mental distress--his entrance into the temple to pray the refuge of a pious man in affliction--and the forwarding an account of the Assyrian's speech to Isaiah was to obtain the prophet's counsel and comfort. The expression in which the message was conveyed described, by a strong figure, the desperate condition of the kingdom, together with their own inability to help themselves; and it intimated also a hope, that the blasphemous defiance of Jehovah's power by the impious Assyrian might lead to some direct interposition for the vindication of His honor and supremacy to all heathen gods. <div eID="gen5031" type="x-p"/>
entries.b63125dbff2bab2fafb5c68a3af7e845b9710241: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3540"/><div sID="gen5032" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3540"/><hi type="bold">4. the living God--</hi>"The living God" is a most significant expression taken in connection with the senseless deities that Rab-shakeh boasted were unable to resist his master's victorious arms.<div eID="gen5032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5033" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.6">2Ki 19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.7">7</reference>. Comforted by Isaiah. <div eID="gen5033" type="x-p"/>
entries.c409e55e1d8a099cb74c1e5dbc3029f6e0602fd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3541"/><div sID="gen5034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3541"/><hi type="bold">6. Isaiah said ... Be not afraid--</hi>The prophet's answer was most cheering, as it held out the prospect of a speedy deliverance from the invader. The blast, the rumor, the fall by the sword, contained a brief prediction that was soon fulfilled in all the three particulars--namely, the alarm that hastened his retreat, the destruction that overtook his army, and the violent death that suddenly ended his career.<div eID="gen5034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5035" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.8-2Kgs.19.13">2Ki 19:8-13</reference>. Sennacherib Sends a Blasphemous Letter to Hezekiah. <div eID="gen5035" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e65e656af770fdc2d7ef80aeb6d8f18266d280f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3542"/><div sID="gen5036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3542"/><hi type="bold">8. So Rab-shakeh ... found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah--</hi>Whether Lachish had fallen or not, is not said. But Sennacherib had transferred his battering-rams against the apparently neighboring fortress of Libnah (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.29">Jos 10:29</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Josh.10.31">Jos 10:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.15.42">15:42</reference>), where the chief-cup-bearer reported the execution of his mission. <div eID="gen5036" type="x-p"/>
entries.67d799767aab6d983bc6b7b71da91461225971e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3543"/><div sID="gen5037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3543"/><hi type="bold">9-13. when he heard say of Tirhakah ..., Behold, he is come out to fight against thee, &c.--</hi>This was the "rumor" to which Isaiah referred [2Ki 19:7]. Tirhakah reigned in Upper Egypt, while So (or Sabaco) ruled in Lower Egypt. He was a powerful monarch, another Sesostris, and both he and Sabaco have left many monuments of their greatness. The name and figure of Tirhakah receiving war captives, are still seen in the Egyptian temple of Medinet Abou. This was the expected succor which was sneered at by Rab-shakeh as "a bruised reed" (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.21">2Ki 18:21</reference>). Rage against Hezekiah for allying himself with Egypt, or the hope of being better able to meet this attack from the south, induced him, after hearing the rumor of Tirhakah's advance, to send a menacing letter to Hezekiah, in order that he might force the king of Judah to an immediate surrender of his capital. This letter, couched in the same vaunting and imperious style as the speech of Rab-shakeh, exceeded it in blasphemy, and contained a larger enumeration of conquered places, with the view of terrifying Hezekiah and showing him the utter hopelessness of all attempts at resistance.<div eID="gen5037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5038" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14-2Kgs.19.34">2Ki 19:14-34</reference>. Hezekiah's Prayer. <div eID="gen5038" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea56e36d9cef30a04730bca03673cb988f969b76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3544"/><div sID="gen5039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3544"/><hi type="bold">14-19. Hezekiah received the letter ... and went up into the house of the Lord--</hi>Hezekiah, after reading it, hastened into the temple, spread it in the childlike confidence of faith before the Lord, as containing taunts deeply affecting the divine honor, and implored deliverance from this proud defier of God and man. The devout spirit of this prayer, the recognition of the Divine Being in the plenitude of His majesty--so strikingly contrasted with the fancy of the Assyrians as to His merely local power; his acknowledgment of the conquests obtained over other lands; and of the destruction of their wooden idols which, according to the Assyrian practice, were committed to the flames--because their tutelary deities were no gods; and the object for which he supplicated the divine interposition--that all the kingdoms of the earth might know that the Lord was the only God--this was an attitude worthy to be assumed by a pious theocratic king of the chosen people. <div eID="gen5039" type="x-p"/>
entries.8299a1a48a6a136a5d91b526ebe845900905bc0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3545"/><div sID="gen5040" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3545"/><hi type="bold">20. Then Isaiah ... sent--</hi>A revelation having been made to Isaiah, the prophet announced to the king that his prayer was heard. The prophetic message consisted of three different portions:--First, Sennacherib is apostrophized (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21-2Kgs.19.28">2Ki 19:21-28</reference>) in a highly poetical strain, admirably descriptive of the turgid vanity, haughty pretensions, and presumptuous impiety of the Assyrian despot. Secondly, Hezekiah is addressed (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.29-2Kgs.19.31">2Ki 19:29-31</reference>), and a sign is given him of the promised deliverance--namely, that for two years the presence of the enemy would interrupt the peaceful pursuits of husbandry, but in the third year the people would be in circumstances to till their fields and vineyards and reap the fruits as formerly. Thirdly, the issue of Sennacherib's invasion is announced (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.32-2Kgs.19.34">2Ki 19:32-34</reference>). <div eID="gen5040" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1fab1edefc8f8dd38684538421136a09ea7f0a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3546"/><div sID="gen5041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3546"/><hi type="bold">33. shall not come into this city--</hi>nor approach near enough to shoot an arrow, not even from the most powerful engine which throws missiles to the greatest distance, nor shall he occupy any part of the ground before the city by a fence, a mantelet, or covering for men employed in a siege, nor cast (raise) a bank (mound) of earth, overtopping the city walls, whence he may see and command the interior of the city. None of these, which were the principal modes of attack followed in ancient military art, should Sennacherib be permitted to adopt. Though the army under Rab-shakeh marched towards Jerusalem and encamped at a little distance with a view to blockade it, they delayed laying siege to it, probably waiting till the king, having taken Lachish and Libnah, should bring up his detachment, that with all the combined forces of Assyria they might invest the capital. So determined was this invader to conquer Judah and the neighboring countries (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Is 10:7</reference>), that nothing but a divine interposition could have saved Jerusalem. It might be supposed that the powerful monarch who overran Palestine and carried away the tribes of Israel, would leave memorials of his deeds on sculptured slabs, or votive bulls. A long and minute account of this expedition is contained in the Annals of Sennacherib, a translation of which has recently been made into English, and, in his remarks upon it, Colonel Rawlinson says the Assyrian version confirms the most important features of the Scripture account. The Jewish and Assyrian narratives of the campaign are, indeed, on the whole, strikingly illustrative of each other [Outlines of Assyrian History].<div eID="gen5041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5042" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Ki 19:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.36">36</reference>. An Angel Destroys the Assyrians. <div eID="gen5042" type="x-p"/>
entries.3369263d672e4107579348d8b129230dc12c357b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3547"/><div sID="gen5043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3547"/><hi type="bold">35. in the morning ... they were all dead corpses--</hi>It was the miraculous interposition of the Almighty that defended Jerusalem. As to the secondary agent employed in the destruction of the Assyrian army, it is most probable that it was effected by a hot south wind, the simoon, such as to this day often envelops and destroys whole caravans. This conjecture is supported by <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.7">2Ki 19:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.51.1">Jr 51:1</reference>. The destruction was during the night; the officers and soldiers, being in full security, were negligent; their discipline was relaxed; the camp guards were not alert, or perhaps they themselves were the first taken off, and those who slept, not wrapped up, imbibed the poison plentifully. If this had been an evening of dissolute mirth (no uncommon thing in a camp), their joy (perhaps for a victory), or "the first night of their attacking the city," says Josephus, became, by its effects, one means of their destruction [Calmet, Fragments]. <div eID="gen5043" type="x-p"/>
entries.015a016186b8ce3dd50fcdefbd67b378773afa67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3548"/><div sID="gen5044" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3548"/><hi type="bold">36. So Sennacherib king of Assyria ... went and returned--</hi>the same way as he came (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.33">2Ki 19:33</reference>). The route is described (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.28-Isa.10.32">Is 10:28-32</reference>). The early chariot track near Beyrout is on the rocky edge of Lebanon, which is skirted by the ancient Lycus (Nahr-el Kelb). On the perpendicular face of the limestone rock, at different heights, are seen slabs with Assyrian inscriptions, which having been deciphered, are found to contain the name of Sennacherib. Thus, by the preservation of these tablets, the wrath of the Assyrian invaders is made to praise the Lord.<div eID="gen5044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelt at Nineveh--</hi>This statement implies a considerable period of time, and his Annals carry on his history at least five years after his disastrous campaign at Jerusalem. No record of his catastrophe can be found, as the Assyrian practice was to record victories alone. The sculptures give only the sunny side of the picture.<div eID="gen5045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5046" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.37">2Ki 19:37</reference>. Sennacherib Slain. <div eID="gen5046" type="x-p"/>
entries.a14cf72ba28757a23ce5a5a2e825a8b593ffde48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3549"/><div sID="gen5047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3549"/><hi type="bold">37. as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch--</hi>Assarae, or Asshur, the head of the Assyrian Pantheon, represented not as a vulture-headed figure (that is now ascertained to be a priest), but as a winged figure in a circle, which was the guardian deity of Assyria. The king is represented on the monuments standing or kneeling beneath this figure, his hand raised in sign of prayer or adoration.<div eID="gen5047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his sons smote him with the sword--</hi>Sennacherib's temper, exasperated probably by his reverses, displayed itself in the most savage cruelty and intolerable tyranny over his subjects and slaves, till at length he was assassinated by his two sons, whom, it is said, he intended to sacrifice to pacify the gods and dispose them to grant him a return of prosperity. The parricides taking flight into Armenia, a third son, Esar-haddon, ascended the throne. <chapter eID="2Kgs.19"/>

entries.395c3ff9e9f0c0ff5ff694bfb634ed5c1a6991cc: <div eID="gen13081" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13082" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13083" type="x-p"/> Hezekiah as greatly distressed, and sends to Isaiah to pray for him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.1-2Kgs.19.4">2Kgs 19:1-4</reference>. Isaiah returns a comfortable answer, and predicts the destruction of the king of Assyria and his army, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.5-2Kgs.19.8">2Kgs 19:5-8</reference>. Sennacherib, hearing that his kingdom was invaded by the Ethiopians, sends a terrible letter to Hezekiah, to induce him to surrender, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.9-2Kgs.19.13">2Kgs 19:9-13</reference>. Hezekiah goes to the temple, spreads the letter before the Lord, and makes a most affecting prayer, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14-2Kgs.19.19">2Kgs 19:14-19</reference>. Isaiah is sent to him to assure him that his prayer is heard; that Jerusalem shall be delivered; and that the Assyrians shall be destroyed, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.20-2Kgs.19.34">2Kgs 19:20-34</reference>. That very night a messenger of God slays one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Kgs 19:35</reference>. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, and is slain by his own sons, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.36">2Kgs 19:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.37">2Kgs 19:37</reference>.
entries.4deab5cb9d9b4f0f6e3ab4960ecca19c88d3e35c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13083" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13082" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13084" type="x-p"/> To Isaiah the prophet - His fame and influence were at this time great in Israel; and it was well known that the word of the Lord was with him. Here both the Church and the state unite in fervent application to, and strong dependence upon, God; and behold how they succeed!
entries.b3d23327fa9a7f64131946e385cf0ee261b2225d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen13084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13085" type="x-p"/> The children are come to the birth - The Jewish state is here represented under the emblem of a woman in travail, who has been so long in the pangs of parturition, that her strength is now entirely exhausted, and her deliverance is hopeless, without a miracle. The image is very fine and highly appropriate. <div eID="gen13085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13086" type="x-p"/> A similar image is employed by Homer, when he represents the agonies which Agamemnon suffers from his wound: - Οφρα οἱ αἱμ' ετι θερμον ανηνοθεν εξ ωτειλης· Λυταρ επει το μεν ἑλκος ετερσετο παυσατο δ' αἱμα, Οξειαι οδυναι δυνον μενος Ατρειδαο· Ως δ' ὁταν ωδινουσαν εχῃ βελος οξυ γυναικα, Δριμυ, το τε προΐεισι μογοστοκοι Ειλειθυιαι Ἡρης θυγατερες πικ ρας ωδινας εχουσαι· Ὡς οξει' οδυναι δυνον μενος Ατρειδαο. <div eID="gen13086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13087" type="x-p"/> Il. xi., ver. 266. <div eID="gen13087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13088" type="x-p"/> This, while yet warm, distill'd the purple flood; <div eID="gen13088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13089" type="x-p"/> But when the wound grew stiff with clotted blood, <div eID="gen13089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13090" type="x-p"/> Then grinding tortures his strong bosom rend. <div eID="gen13090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13091" type="x-p"/> Less keen those darts the fierce Ilythiae send, <div eID="gen13091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13092" type="x-p"/> The powers that cause the teeming matron's throes, <div eID="gen13092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13093" type="x-p"/> Sad mothers of unutterable woes. <div eID="gen13093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13094" type="x-p"/> Pope <div eID="gen13094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13095" type="x-p"/> Better translated by Macpherson; but in neither well: "So long as from the gaping wound gushed forth, in its warmth, the blood; but when the wound became dry, when ceased the blood to flow amain, sharp pains pervade the strength of Atrides. Racking pangs glide through his frame; as when the Ilythiae, who preside over births, the daughters of white armed Juno, fierce dealers of bitter pains, throw all their darts on hapless women, that travail with child. Such pains pervade the strength of Atrides."
entries.6cbeed9893380522f9dea6a79d6fbac8cdc62e55: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen13095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13096" type="x-p"/> The remnant that are left - That is, the Jews; the ten tribes having been already carried away captive by the kings of Assyria.
entries.bf94723c59f72e01f8f561b09cda251e46c17a82: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen13096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13097" type="x-p"/> Behold, I will send a blast - and he shall hear a rumor - The rumor was, that Tirhakah had invaded Assyria. The blast was that which slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand of them in one night, see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Kgs 19:35</reference>. <div eID="gen13097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13098" type="x-p"/> Cause him to fall by the sword - Alluding to his death by the hands of his two sons, at Nineveh. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35-2Kgs.19.37">2Kgs 19:35-37</reference>.
entries.5959335ac2cb15150e2787645fa3956adaeee447: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen13098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13099" type="x-p"/> Libnah - Lachish - These two places were not very distant from each other; they were in the mountains of Judah, southward of Jerusalem.
entries.e75734a291eef16d9fb8afe85dabf97720988b24: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen13099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13100" type="x-p"/> Let not thy God in whom thou trustest - This letter is nearly the same with the speech delivered by Rab-shakeh. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.29">2Kgs 18:29</reference>.
entries.a0ae8f878cee9a2c59cef787bb9a4ea88408f46d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen13100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13101" type="x-p"/> Spread it before the Lord - The temple was considered to be God's dwelling-place; and that whatever was there was peculiarly under his eye. Hezekiah spread the letter before the Lord, as he wished him to read the blasphemies spoken against himself.
entries.8ea3d7b5fd5c1a578934abcf62ab0c1063ae5d64: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen13101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13102" type="x-p"/> Thou art the God, etc. - Thou art not only God of Israel, but God also of Assyria, and of all the nations of the world.
entries.52d463b404744f34a1a4292ae618e7622c622608: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen13102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13103" type="x-p"/> The virgin the daughter of Zion hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee - "So truly contemptible is thy power, and empty thy boasts, that even the young women of Jerusalem, under the guidance of Jehovah, shall be amply sufficient to discomfit all thy forces, and cause thee to return with shame to thy own country, where the most disgraceful death awaits thee." When Bishop Warburton had published his Doctrine of Grace, and chose to fall foul on some of the most religious people of the land, a young woman of the city of Gloucester exposed his graceless system in a pamphlet, to which she affixed the above words as a motto!
entries.ae7ebeabbc280784b60b591335bd629efa42dc95: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen13103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13104" type="x-p"/> The tall cedar trees - the choice fir trees - Probably meaning the princes and nobles of the country. <div eID="gen13104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13105" type="x-p"/> The forest of his Carmel - Better in the margin: the forest and his fruitful field.
entries.ae9e396136cfb112288a3410c9bef6d0fa122225: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen13105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13106" type="x-p"/> I have dipped and drunk strange waters - I have conquered strange countries, in which I have digged wells for my army; or, I have gained the wealth of strange countries. <div eID="gen13106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13107" type="x-p"/> With the sole of my feet - My infantry have been so numerous that they alone have been sufficient to drink up the rivers of the places I have besieged.
entries.b9d58bcc6201b4f0fa02a6feec213af8dde6bb0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen13107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13108" type="x-p"/> Hast thou not heard - Here Jehovah speaks, and shows this boasting king that what he had done was done by the Divine appointment, and that of his own counsel and might he could have done nothing. It was because God had appointed them to this civil destruction that he had overcome them; and it was not through his might; for God had made their inhabitants of small power, so that he only got the victory over men whom God had confounded, dismayed, and enervated, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.26">2Kgs 19:26</reference>.
entries.61c206e80e4a4c53fea027fe74f9674829ca7230: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen13108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13109" type="x-p"/> I will put my hook in thy nose - This seems to be an allusion to the method of guiding a buffalo; he has a sort of ring put into his nose, to which a cord or bridle is attached, by which he can be turned to the right, or to the left, or round about, according to the pleasure of his driver.
entries.3897fd62384512f450f13501585e639ced567575: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen13109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13110" type="x-p"/> This shall be a sign unto thee - To Hezekiah; for to him this part of the address is made. <div eID="gen13110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13111" type="x-p"/> Ye shall eat this year - Sennacherib had ravaged the country, and seed-time was now over, yet God shows them that he would so bless the land, that what should grow of itself that year, would be quite sufficient to supply the inhabitants and prevent all famine; and though the second year was the sabbatical rest or jubilee for the land, in which it was unlawful to plough or sow; yet even then the land, by an especial blessing of God, should bring forth a sufficiency for its inhabitants; and in the third year they should sow and plant, etc. and have abundance, etc. Now this was to be a sign to Hezekiah, that his deliverance had not been effected by natural or casual means; for as without a miracle the ravaged and uncultivated land could not yield food for its inhabitants, so not without miraculous interference could the Assyrian army be cut off and Israel saved.
entries.9fcff2a2cdffaac39baf48d1e8a038148caf51b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen13111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13112" type="x-p"/> The remnant - shall yet again take root - As your corn shall take root in the soil, and bring forth and abundantly multiply itself, so shall the Jewish people; the population shall be greatly increased, and the desolations occasioned by the sword soon be forgotten.
entries.d9847988b5eae65a950ff52c805232365c9bd6db: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen13112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13113" type="x-p"/> Out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant - The Jews shall be so multiplied as not only to fill Jerusalem, but all the adjacent country. <div eID="gen13113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13114" type="x-p"/> And they that escape out of Mount Zion - Some think that this refers to the going forth of the apostles to the Gentile world, and converting the nations by the preaching of the Gospel.
entries.e97a1af4162a2ecd761578d934e3df9a2feac2ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen13114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13115" type="x-p"/> He shall not, etc. - Here follow the fullest proofs that Jerusalem shall not be taken by the Assyrians. <div eID="gen13115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13116" type="x-p"/> 1. He shall not come into this city; <div eID="gen13116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13117" type="x-p"/> 2. He shall not be able to get so near as to shoot an arrow into it; <div eID="gen13117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13118" type="x-p"/> 3. He shall not be able to bring an army before it, <div eID="gen13118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13119" type="x-p"/> 4. Nor shall he be able to raise any redoubt or mound against it; <div eID="gen13119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13120" type="x-p"/> 5. No; not even an Assyrian shield shall be seen in the country; not even a foraging party shall come near the city.
entries.80c65c17f3058941c0d7686af26a74d29a7c7bd5: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen13120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13121" type="x-p"/> By the way that he came - Though his army shall not return, yet he shall return to Assyria; for because of his blasphemy he is reserved for a more ignominious death.
entries.7018efa860374079f4db1afdf5b84b1edd6a22d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen13121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13122" type="x-p"/> That night - The very night after the blasphemous message had been sent, and this comfortable prophecy delivered. <div eID="gen13122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13123" type="x-p"/> The angel of the Lord went out - I believe this angel or messenger of the Lord was simply a suffocating or pestilential Wind; by which the Assyrian army was destroyed, as in a moment, without noise confusion or any warning. See the note <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.30">1Kgs 20:30</reference>. Thus was the threatening, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.7">2Kgs 19:7</reference>, fulfilled, I will send a Blast upon him; for he had heard the rumor that his territories were invaded; and on his way to save his empire, in one night the whole of his army was destroyed, without any one even seeing who had hurt them. This is called an angel or messenger of the Lord: that is, something immediately sent by him to execute his judgments. <div eID="gen13123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13124" type="x-p"/> When they arose early - That is, Sennacherib, and probably a few associates, who were preserved as witnesses and relaters of this most dire disaster. Rab-shakeh, no doubt, perished with the rest of the army.
entries.702d5198714f07441971fbdd7d7cfd74c098b54f: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen13124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13125" type="x-p"/> Dwelt at Nineveh - This was the capital of the Assyrian empire.
entries.07b4f3975962ec4c73ed90ca7a96fe1258f34aa4: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen13125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13126" type="x-p"/> Nisroch his god - We know nothing of this deity; he is nowhere else mentioned. <div eID="gen13126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13127" type="x-p"/> Smote him with the sword - The rabbins say that his sons had learned that he intended to sacrifice them to this god, and that they could only prevent this by slaying him. <div eID="gen13127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13128" type="x-p"/> The same writers add, that he consulted his wise men how it was that such miracles should be wrought for the Israelites; who told him that it was because of the merit of Abraham who had offered his only son to God: he then said, I will offer to him my two sons; which when they heard, they rose up and slew him. When a rabbin cannot untie a knot, he feels neither scruple nor difficulty to cut it.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.19"/> <div eID="gen13128" type="x-p"/>

entries.d5f1e3a0ec792e30fab71182f887b8d8382d9e7a: 2Ki 19:1-2 <div eID="gen5411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5412" type="x-p"/> When Hezekiah had heard from his counsellors the report of Rabshakeh’s words, he rent his clothes with horror at his daring mockery of the living God (2Ki 19:4), put on mourning clothes as a sign of the trouble of his soul and went into the temple, and at the same time sent Eliakim and Shebna with the oldest of the priests in mourning costume to the prophet Isaiah, to entreat him to intercede with the Lord in these desperate circumstances.<note placement="foot">“But the most wise king did not meet his blasphemies with weapons, but with prayer, and tears, and sackcloth, and entreated the prophet Isaiah to be his ambassador.” - Theodoret.</note> <div eID="gen5412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5413" type="x-p"/> The order of the words: Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, is unusual (cf. 2Ki 14:25; 2Ki 20:1; 1Ki 16:7, etc.), and is therefore altered in Isaiah into Isaiah the son of Amoz, the prophet.
entries.33291ac6d668de5db71ba6e9899f85c390f189d7: 2Ki 19:3 “A day of distress, and of chastisement, and of rejection is this day.” תּוכחה: the divine chastisement. נאצה: contemptuous treatment, or rejection of the people on the part of God (compare נאץ, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.19">Deu 32:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">Jer 14:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.6">Lam 2:6</reference>). “For children have come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth.” A figure denoting extreme danger, the most desperate circumstances. If the woman in travail has not strength to bring forth the child which has come to the mouth of the womb, both the life of the child and that of the mother are exposed to the greatest danger; and this was the condition of the people here (see the similar figure in Hos 13:13). For לדה instead of לדת, see Ges. §69, 2 Anm.
entries.23d126a3523d770d68b4ed57751495b66f9c214c: 2Ki 19:4 <div eID="gen5413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5414" type="x-p"/> Perhaps Jehovah thy God will hear the blasphemies of the living God on the part of Rabshakeh. ישׁמע: hear, equivalent to observes, take notice of, and in this case punish. חי אלהים: the living God, in contrast to the gods of the heathen, who are only lifeless idols (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.26">1Sa 17:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.36">1Sa 17:36</reference>). והוכיח is not to be taken in connection with לחרף, as if it stood for להוכיח, “and to scold with words” (Luth., Ges., etc.), but is a perf. rel. or a progressive perfect (Ewald, §234, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.), and the continuation of ישׁמע: “and will chastise (punish, sc. him) for the words which He has heard.” תף ונשׂאת “therefore lift up prayer (to heaven) for the (still) existing remnant, sc. of the people of God;” nearly all Judah having come into the power of Sennacherib since the carrying away of the ten tribes.
entries.3b450178d2386f3debaa51468e91af08c3f339b0: 2Ki 19:5-7 <div eID="gen5414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5415" type="x-p"/> Isaiah replied with this comforting promise: Hezekiah was not to be afraid of the blasphemous words of the Assyrian king; the Lord would frighten him with a report, so that he would return to his own land, and there would He cause him to fall by the sword. מלך א נערי, the servants or young men of the Assyrian king, is a derogatory epithet applied to the officials of Assyria. “Behold, I put a spirit into him, so that he shall hear a report and return into his own land.” שׁמוּעה does not refer to the report of the destruction of his army (2Ki 19:35), as Thenius supposes, for Sennacherib did not hear of this through the medium of an army, but was with the army himself at the time when it was smitten by the angel of the Lord; it refers to the report mentioned in 2Ki 19:9. For even if he made one last attempt to secure the surrender of Jerusalem immediately upon hearing this report, yet after the failure of this attempt to shake the firmness of Hezekiah his courage must have failed him, and the thought of return must have suggested itself, so that this was only accelerated by the blow which fell upon the army. For, as O. v. Gerlach has correctly observed, “the destruction of the army would hardly have produced any decisive effect without the approach of Tirhakah, since the great power of the Assyrian king, especially in relation to the small kingdom of Judah, was not broken thereby. But at the prayer of the king the Lord added this miracle to the other, which His providence had already brought to pass. - For the fulfilment of the prophecy of Sennacherib’s death, see 2Ki 19:37.
entries.4611e532e005de3d55bc3b24cd1792972c8960d3: 2Ki 19:8 <div eID="gen5415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5416" type="x-p"/> In the meantime Rabshakeh had returned to his king at Libnah (see at 2Ki 8:22), to which he had gone from Lachish, probably after having taken that fortress.
entries.1e2286f237aa49e1ad00739459df7589990cf149: 2Ki 19:9 <div eID="gen5416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5417" type="x-p"/> There Sennacherib heard that Tirhakah was advancing to make war against him. Tirhakah, Θαρακά (lxx), king of Cush, is the Ταρακός of Manetho, the successor of Sevechus (Shebek II), the third king of the twenty-fifth (Ethiopian) dynasty, described by Strabo (xv. 687), who calls him Τεάρκων, as a great conqueror. His name is spelt <hi type="italic">Tåhålqa</hi> or <hi type="italic">Tåharqo</hi> upon the monuments, and on the Pylon of the great temple at Medinet-Abu he is represented in the form of a king, cutting down enemies of conquered lands (Egypt, Syria, and <hi type="italic">Tepopå</hi>, an unknown land) before the god Ammon (see Brugsch, <hi type="italic">hist. d'Egypte</hi>, i. pp. 244,245).<note placement="foot">According to Jul. Afric. (in Syncell. i. p. 139, ed. Dind.) he reigned eighteen years, according to Euseb. (in Syncell. p. 140) twenty years.
